text: Observations. In every group of class \(c\) computed, \(D_{c+1}=1\) and \(D_k=\gamma_k\) at each step. For metabelian groups of class \(3\) the Jennings sieve removes almost everything (orders \(64\), \(128\), \(256\), \(512\): \(111/114\), \(1116/1137\), \(21\,105/21\,325\), \(1\,584\,597/1\,587\,389\)), and the survivors have \(D_4=1\) already. For \(3\)-groups of class \(4\) the sieve removes little (\(9/71\) at order \(729\), \(107/1309\) at order \(2187\)). Computing time: about \(3.6\) hours wall clock, about \(30\)–\(40\) CPU-hours.

Remark (pruning the generation tree; D5-25). Let \(Q\) be a finite \(2\)-group of class \(3\) with cyclic centre, \(d=d(Q)\), \(C=C_Q(\gamma_2(Q))\), \(X=\gamma_2(Q)/(\gamma_2(Q)\cap Z(Q))\). The commutator map \(X\times Q/C\to\gamma_3(Q)\) is a non-degenerate bilinear pairing into the cyclic group \(\gamma_3(Q)\le Z(Q)\); hence \(X\cong Q/C\), a quotient of \(Q_{ab}\), and \(X\) has rank \(\le\min(d,d(d-1)/2)\). If \(|\gamma_3(Q)|=2^e\), then \(Q_{ab}\) has two invariants \(\ge 2^e\) (the map \((u,v)\mapsto[u,v,z]\) factors through \(\Lambda^2Q_{ab}\)) and \(X\) has an element of order \(\ge 2^e\). For a minimal counterexample \(Q\) (Lemma 5.2) with central involution \(n\) this gives conditions on every quotient \(V=Q/N\) with \(N\le\Phi(Q)\) (with \(n\in N\le\Phi(Q)\) for the second), which pass to further quotients and so may be used to cut whole subtrees of the \(p\)-group generation tree: (i) there is a cyclic \(K\), \(\gamma_3(V)\le K\le\gamma_2(V)\cap Z(V)\), with \(\mathrm{rk}(\gamma_2(V)/K)\le\min(d,d(d-1)/2)\); (ii) for such a \(K\), \(|Q|\ge 2|K|\,|A\vee B\vee E_1|\,|A\vee V_{ab}\vee E_2|\), where \(A=\gamma_2(V)/K\), \(B=V/C_V(\gamma_2(V))\), \(E_1=\mathbb{Z}/2^{e_V+1}\), \(E_2=E_1^2\), \(2^{e_V}=|\gamma_3(V)|\), and \(\vee\) is the componentwise maximum of abelian invariants. In particular every such \(V\) of class \(3\) has \(d+4e_V+2\le\log_2|Q|\). [paper] (proofs in compute/pq2048/README.md). Condition (i) is vacuous for \(d\le3\) and below order \(2^{2d+1}\); condition (ii) is the one that cuts.

Order \(2^{11}\), ranks \(2\)–\(7\). At order \(2^{11}\) the same argument needs as parents the groups of order \(2^{10}\) of class \(\le3\) with cyclic \(\gamma_3\); they are not in SmallGroups, and a rough extrapolation puts their number at \(0.5\)–\(1.1\cdot10^9\). Remark 5.5 cuts whole subtrees without losing a candidate (checked: the same \(3\), \(11\), \(64\), \(308\) candidates at orders \(2^6\)–\(2^9\)) and leaves, by a sample, \(10^5\)–\(2\cdot10^6\) parents; generating them is still about \(100\) CPU-days, mostly rank \(5\) [computer; estimate] (made before rules (A), (B), (T) below; rank \(5\) then took about \(83\) CPU-hours). Ranks \(2\)–\(7\) have been run through to order \(2^{11}\): \(17\), \(586\), \(52\,568\), \(824\), \(13\) and \(9\) candidates (at ranks \(5\) and \(6\) after rule (T) below), all with \(D_4=D_5=1\) [computer]. For rank \(4\) the walk passes through \(2\,756\) candidates at order \(2^{10}\), exactly the rank-\(4\) count of Proposition 5.3; it kept \(52\,181\) parents of order \(2^{10}\) (and cut \(9\,937\), \(136\,127\), \(946\,663\) vertices at orders \(2^8\), \(2^9\), \(2^{10}\)) and took about \(15\) CPU-hours for the tree and \(4.6\) for the lattices (code: compute/pq2048, run_rank.sh). The pruned search used there was checked at order \(2^{10}\), where it reproduces the \(3400\) candidates of Proposition 5.3 exactly, rank by rank, while keeping \(4.2\%\) of the parents. Ranks \(5\) and \(6\) used, on top of Remark 5.5, three more rules; proofs and references are in compute/pq2048/README.md, section “Rules of the rank-5 and rank-6 runs”. (A) A vertex of order \(2^9\), \(2\)-class \(2\) and elementary abelianization is not expanded: it is not a parent, its steps \(\ge2\) go past order \(2^{10}\), and its step-\(1\) descendants all have class \(3\) and fail the bound of Remark 5.5(ii) [paper]. (B) The step-\(1\) descendants of class \(3\) of a vertex of order \(2^9\) and \(2\)-class \(2\) whose abelianization has fewer than two invariants \(\ge4\) are dropped, as they fail the same bound [paper]. (T) A leaf of order \(2^{10}\) whose abelianization has at most one invariant \(\ge4\) is dropped: a candidate \(Q\) above it has the same abelianization, so \(D_4(Q)=\gamma_4(Q)=1\) by Tahara's Corollary 19 [Tah77a, p. 125] (for a \(2\)-group of class \(3\) whose abelianization has at most one cyclic factor of order \(\ge4\), \(D_4=\gamma_4\); Tahara attributes it to Passi [Pas79, Thm. 10.1]) and hence \(D_5(Q)=1\) [paper]. Rules (A) and (B) lose no candidate. Rule (T) does drop candidates, but only ones with \(D_5=1\), so the rank-\(5\) and rank-\(6\) counts above are of the candidates left after it; a rank-\(6\) run that applied (T) to only part of its pieces kept \(469\) candidates, all with \(D_4=D_5=1\) [computer]. These two ranks were run with ANUPQ with the fixes of the audit mentioned in Section 6, and with automorphism groups not computed for descendants that are leaves (an option proposed upstream as gap-packages/anupq#124; on \(283\) test groups the build used gives the same \(35\,213\) descendants as without the option [computer]). Ranks \(2\)–\(4\) and \(7\), like the order-\(2^{10}\) search of Proposition 5.3, were first run with ANUPQ before those fixes (two of the fixed defects can change the descendants) and then repeated with the same fixed build: the results agree exactly, namely all \(858\) chunk tables and the \(3400\) candidates with their lattice answers at order \(2^{10}\), and the candidates of ranks \(2\)–\(4\) and \(7\) at order \(2^{11}\); so does the direct generation at rank \(8\) described after Proposition 5.7 [computer]. For rank \(5\) the walk passes through \(319\) candidates at order \(2^{10}\), and for rank \(6\) through \(9\), again exactly the counts of Proposition 5.3; rank \(5\) kept \(206\,519\) parents of order \(2^{10}\) and took about \(83\) CPU-hours for the tree and minutes for the lattices. At rank \(7\) the stock ANUPQ fails with an integer overflow on the step-\(2\) descendants of \((\mathbb{Z}/2)^7\); these are the \(1\,112\) groups of order \(2^9\), rank \(7\) and \(2\)-class \(2\), a contiguous block of SmallGroups (by SmallGroupsInformation), and the walk starts from them. Ranks \(\ge8\) need no search (Proposition 5.7 below); so order \(2^{11}\) is settled (Proposition 5.10).

Order \(2^{11}\), rank \(\ge8\). Call a \(2\)-group \(Q\) a candidate if it has class \(3\), cyclic centre with involution \(n\in\gamma_3(Q)\cap M_5(Q)\), and \(2\)-class \(c\ge4\) with \(P_c(Q)=\langle n\rangle\). By Lemma 5.2 and Proposition 5.3, a \(2\)-group of order \(2^{11}\) and class \(3\) with \(D_5\ne1\) is a candidate (its quotients by central subgroups of order \(2\) have order \(2^{10}\) and class \(\le3\)).

Proposition. [[computer + paper], via Proposition 5.3; the statement on candidates: [paper], and that no candidate has \(|P_2(Q)|\le8\): [Lean]; the \(D_5\) statement given Proposition 5.3 and \(D_3=\gamma_3\): [Lean]] \(D_5(Q)=1\) for every \(2\)-group \(Q\) of order \(2^{11}\), class \(3\) and rank \(d(Q)\ge8\). More generally, every candidate \(Q\) has \(|\Phi(Q)|\ge16\), that is, \(d(Q)\le\log_2|Q|-4\).

Proof. The first statement follows from the second: a counterexample would be a candidate (see above) with \(|\Phi(Q)|=2^{11-d}\le8\). Let \(Q\) be a candidate with \(|\Phi(Q)|\le8\). The series \(P_i\) decreases strictly until it reaches \(1\) (if \(P_{i+1}=P_i\), it is constant from \(i\) on), and \(\Phi(Q)=P_2\) (Burnside); since \(c\ge4\), \(P_2\supsetneq P_3\supsetneq P_4\supseteq P_c=\langle n\rangle\) gives \(|P_2|=8\), \(|P_3|=4\) and \(P_4=\langle n\rangle\). Also \(\gamma_2\le P_2\), \(\gamma_3\le P_3\), and \(\gamma_3\) is central since \(\gamma_4=1\); so \([u^m,g]=[u,g]^m\) for \(u\in\gamma_2\), \(g\in Q\), and \(\gamma_3\) is generated by the \([u,g]\). As in step (2) of the proof of Lemma 5.6, \(\gamma_3\ne1\) and \(\gamma_3\ne\gamma_2\), so \(|\gamma_2|\ge4\). Since \(\gamma_4=1\), \(M_5(Q)=Q^8\gamma_2^4\gamma_3^2\), and the generators \(x^8\), \(y^4\) (\(y\in\gamma_2\le P_2\)) and \(z^2\) (\(z\in\gamma_3\le P_3\)) of the three factors lie in \(P_4=\{1,n\}\). As \(n\in M_5(Q)\), one of them equals \(n\).

(a) \(z^2=n\) for some \(z\in\gamma_3\). Then \(z\) has order \(4\), so \(\gamma_3=P_3=\langle z\rangle\) is central. For \(u\in\gamma_2\) and \(g\in Q\) we have \(u^2\in P_3\), hence \([u,g]^2=[u^2,g]=1\) and \([u,g]\in\langle z^2\rangle=\langle n\rangle\). So \(\gamma_3\le\langle n\rangle\), contradicting \(z^2=n\ne1\).

(b) \(y^4=n\) for some \(y\in\gamma_2\). Then \(y\) has order \(8\), so \(\gamma_2=P_2=\langle y\rangle\) and \(P_3=\langle y^2\rangle\). For \(g\in Q\), \([y,g]^2=[y^2,g]\in[P_3,Q]\le P_4=\langle n\rangle\). If \([y,g]^2=n\), then \([y,g]\in\gamma_3\) has order \(4\), so \(\langle[y,g]\rangle=P_3\ni y^2\), and \(y^2\in\gamma_3\) is central: \([y^2,g]=1\), a contradiction. Hence \([y,g]^2=1\), that is, \([y,g]\in\langle y^4\rangle=\langle n\rangle\), and \(\gamma_3\), generated by the \([y^m,g]=[y,g]^m\), lies in \(\langle n\rangle\). Now let \(g,h\in Q\). Since \(g^2\in P_2=\gamma_2\), we have \([g^2,h]\in\gamma_3\), and \([g^2,h]\equiv[g,h]^2\pmod{\gamma_3}\); so \([g,h]^2\in\gamma_3\le\langle n\rangle\), \([g,h]^4=1\) and \([g,h]\in\langle y^2\rangle\). Then \(\gamma_2\le\langle y^2\rangle\) has order \(\le4\), a contradiction.

(c) \(x^8=n\) for some \(x\in Q\). Then \(x^2\in P_2\) has order \(8\), so \(P_2=\langle x^2\rangle\) is cyclic, and \(\gamma_2\le P_2\) has order \(4\) or \(8\). If \(|\gamma_2|=8\), then \(\gamma_2=P_2\ni x^2\) and \((x^2)^4=n\), which is case (b). If \(|\gamma_2|=4\), then \(\gamma_2=\langle x^4\rangle=P_3\), and steps (2)–(7) of the proof of Lemma 5.6 give a contradiction: they use \(Q/P_3(Q)\) only through \(\gamma_2\le P_3\), \(|P_3|=4\), \(P_4=\langle n\rangle\) and \(Q^4\le P_3\), which holds in every group (\(x^4=(x^2)^2\) with \(x^2\in P_2\)).

The bound is sharp at both searched orders: the candidates of order \(2^{10}\) have rank \(\le6\), with \(9\) of rank \(6\) (Proposition 5.3), and at order \(2^{11}\) there are \(9\) of rank \(7\), while direct generation at rank \(8\) finds none (below).

Checks. The case \(d=8\) (then \(c=4\), \(|P_3(Q)|=4\) and \(P_4(Q)=\langle n\rangle\), as in the first paragraph of the proof) was first settled through \(V=Q/P_3(Q)\), of order \(2^9\), rank \(8\) and \(2\)-class \(2\): \(R=Q/\langle n\rangle\) is an immediate descendant of step \(1\) of \(V\), of class \(2\) by Remark 5.5(ii) (if it had class \(3\), then \(d+4e_R+2\le11\) with \(e_R\ge1\), i.e. \(d\le5\)). [computer] The groups of order \(2^9\) and rank \(8\) are the \(12\) groups SmallGroup\((512,i)\), \(10\,494\,201\le i\le10\,494\,212\) (a group \(V\) of rank \(n\) with \(|\Phi(V)|=2\) is determined by its squaring map \(q\colon V/\Phi(V)\to\Phi(V)\), a nonzero quadratic form on \(\mathbb F_2^n\) whose polar form is the commutator form, so such groups correspond to nonzero quadratic forms up to equivalence; if the polar form has rank \(2k\) and radical \(R\), then \(q|_R=0\) gives two classes for each \(1\le k\le n/2\) (Arf invariant \(0\) or \(1\)) and \(q|_R\ne0\) one class for each \(0\le k<n/2\), so \(2\lfloor n/2\rfloor+\lceil n/2\rceil\) classes, \(12\) for \(n=8\); the same formula gives the numbers of groups of order \(2^{n+1}\) and rank \(n\) in SmallGroups for \(n=2,\dots,7\), namely \(3,4,6,7,9,10\)). Of the \(11\) non-abelian ones, \(10\) have trivial nucleus and hence no immediate descendants at all [OBr90]; for SmallGroup\((512,10\,494\,202)\) the nucleus has dimension \(1\), but every immediate descendant of class \(\le3\) has class \(3\), so it has no descendant \(R\) of class \(2\). Both are read off the \(p\)-covering group, without computing automorphism groups; the two rules and their proofs are in compute/pq2048/README.md (section “Vertices without descendants”, Rules \(0\) and \(2\)) [paper], checked there against full ANUPQ expansion. The remaining group SmallGroup\((512,10\,494\,201)\cong\mathbb{Z}/4\times(\mathbb{Z}/2)^7\) is excluded by Lemma 5.6.

An independent check of rank \(8\) by direct generation agrees: on \(\mathbb{Z}/4\times(\mathbb{Z}/2)^7\) the stock ANUPQ is estimated to need about \(20\) GB (a run was killed at \(7\) GB), while a version with a memory fix completes it in \(2.1\) GB, finding \(8\) immediate descendants of order \(2^{10}\); the walk from all \(12\) groups then gives no candidate of order \(2^{11}\) [computer].

Central products. A search beyond order \(2^{11}\) may skip candidates that split as central products with a small factor. Let \(E\) be a finite \(2\)-group of class \(2\) with \(E/Z(E)\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2\) and cyclic centre. Replacing \(E\) by the subgroup generated by two lifts \(a,b\) of a basis of \(E/Z(E)\), which does not change the central product below, one has \(E\in\{D_8,Q_8\}\) or \(E\cong M_{2^{k+2}}=\langle a,b\mid a^{2^{k+1}}=b^2=1,\ a^b=a^{1+2^k}\rangle\), \(k\ge2\), with \(Z(E)=\langle a^2\rangle\) [paper]. For an embedding \(\varphi\colon Z(E)\to Z(H)\) let \(H\circ E=(H\times E)/\{(\varphi(z),z^{-1})\}\), \(t=\varphi([a,b])\) and, for \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\), \(s=\varphi(a^2)\).

Proposition ([Lean]). Let \(H\) be a group with \(t\in\gamma_2(H)\), and \(n\ge2\). • If \(E\in\{D_8,Q_8\}\), then \(D_n(H\circ E)=D_n(H)\). • If \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\) and for some \(g\in H\) the element \(c=g^{-2}s\) satisfies \(c^{2^j}-1\in\Delta(H)^{j+2}\) for all \(j\ge0\) (for instance \(c^{2^j}\in\gamma_{j+2}(H)\)), then \(D_n(H\circ E)=D_n(H)\). This holds in particular if \(s=g^2\) for some \(g\in H\), central or not (\(c=1\)), and if \(s\in\gamma_2(H)\), \(s^2\in\gamma_3(H)\) (\(g=1\), \(k=2\)).

Proof. Let \(Q\ge H\) be one of the groups below, generated by \(H\) and elements commuting with \(H\), and \(\gamma_2(Q)=\gamma_2(H)\). Then \(D_n(Q)\subseteq\gamma_2(Q)\subseteq H\) and \(D_n(H)\subseteq D_n(Q)\), so \(D_n(Q)=D_n(H)\) follows once \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\cap\Delta(Q)^n\subseteq\Delta(H)^n\). For that it suffices to have a left \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\)-linear \(q\colon\mathbb{Z}[Q]\to\mathbb{Z}[H]\), the identity on \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\), with \(q(\Delta(Q)^n)\subseteq\Delta(H)^n\). Here \(\gamma_2(H\circ E)=\gamma_2(H)\langle t\rangle=\gamma_2(H)\).

(1) Let \(E=D_8\), \(c=[a,b]\), \(\tau=c-1\) (so \(\tau^2=-2\tau\)), and \(N=\mathbb{Z}[E/\langle b\rangle]\), free over \(\mathbb{Z}[\langle c\rangle]\) on \(e_0\) and \(f=ae_0-e_0\). Then \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[\langle c\rangle]}N\) is a \(\mathbb{Z}[Q]\)-module, and \(q(u)=(\mathrm{id}\otimes p)(u(1\otimes e_0))\) with \(p(xe_0+yf)=x\) is as required. Indeed, \(\Delta(Q)^n\) is spanned by products of \(i\) factors from \(\Delta(H)\) and \(n-i\) from \(\Delta(E)\), and on \(N\) in the coordinates \((x,y)\) one has \(a-1\colon(x,y)\mapsto(0,x-2y)\) and \(b-1\colon(x,y)\mapsto(\tau y,\tau y)\). By induction, \(p(\Delta(E)^jN)=\tau^{\lceil j/2\rceil}\mathbb{Z}[\langle c\rangle]\) for \(j\ge1\); as \(t-1\in\Delta(H)^2\), \(q(\Delta(Q)^n)\subseteq\sum_i\Delta(H)^i(t-1)^{\lceil(n-i)/2\rceil}\subseteq\Delta(H)^n\). For \(Q_8\): \(u=ab\in D_8\) has \(u^2=t\), so \(H'=H\langle u\rangle\le H\circ D_8\) and \(D_n(H')=D_n(H)\). If \(a',b'\) are the generators of the factor \(D_8\) of \(H'\circ D_8\), the elements \(a'u,b'u\) generate a \(Q_8\) meeting \(H'\) in \(\langle t\rangle\), so \(H\circ Q_8\le H'\circ D_8\) and \(D_n(H\circ Q_8)\subseteq D_n(H')\cap H=D_n(H)\), using (1) for \(H'\).

(2) Let \(H''=H\langle r\rangle\) with \(r\) central, \(r^2=s\), \(\langle r\rangle\cap H=\langle s\rangle\). With \(a',b'\) the generators of the factor \(D_8\) of \(H''\circ D_8\), the elements \(a'r,b'\) generate a copy of \(E\) meeting \(H''\) in \(\langle s\rangle\), and \(H\langle a\rangle\cong H''\) inside \(H\circ E\); by (1), \(D_n(H\circ E)=D_n(H'')\). Now \(\mathbb{Z}[H'']=\mathbb{Z}[H]\oplus\mathbb{Z}[H]r\); put \(q(u_0+u_1r)=u_0+u_1g\). As \(r\) is central, \(\Delta(H'')^n=\sum_i\Delta(H)^{n-i}(r-1)^i\mathbb{Z}[H'']\), so it suffices that \(f_i=q((r-1)^i)\in\Delta(H)^i\) for all \(i\). In the abelian group \(\langle g,s,r\rangle\) put \(y=rg^{-1}\), so \(y^2=c\), and \(x=g-1\), \(\eta=y-1\), \(\tau=c-1\). Then \(r-1=x+\eta+x\eta\) and \(f_i=\sum_{\alpha+\beta\ge i}m_{\alpha\beta}\,x^\alpha e_\beta\) with \(e_b=\pi(\eta^b)\), \(\pi(v_0+v_1y)=v_0+v_1\). From \(\eta^2=\tau-2\eta\) we get \(e_1=0\), \(e_2=\tau\) and \(e_{b+2}=\tau e_b-2e_{b+1}\). The identity \(2(c^{2^j}-1)=(c^{2^{j+1}}-1)-(c^{2^j}-1)^2\) and the hypothesis give \(2^m\tau\in\Delta(H)^{m+2}\) for all \(m\). Hence, by induction on \(b\ge1\), \(2^me_b\in\Delta(H)^{b+m}\) for all \(m\); in particular \(e_b\in\Delta(H)^b\).

The condition \(c\in\gamma_2(H)\), i.e. \(s\in\Phi(H)\) for a \(2\)-group, cannot be dropped from the method: if \(s\notin\Phi(H)\), no such \(q\) for \(H''\) satisfies \(q(\Delta(H'')^2)\subseteq\Delta(H)^2\) [paper]. [computer] For the \(386\) candidates \(H\) of orders \(2^6\)–\(2^9\), \(t=n\in\gamma_3(H)\). The \(291\) with \(|Z(H)|\ge8\) have \(s\) a square in the cyclic \(Z(H)\). Of the \(95\) with \(Z(H)\cong\mathbb{Z}/4\), \(78\) have \(s\in\gamma_2(H)\) and \(s^2\in\gamma_3(H)\), and the other \(17\) have \(s=g^2\) with \(g\in H\) not central. So by Proposition 5.8, \(D_n(H\circ E)=D_n(H)\) for all of them, all \(n\) and \(E\in\{D_8,Q_8,M_{16}\}\). Independently, the lattice computation gives \(D_4=D_5=1\) for all \(1\,544\) such products.

Gluing along a proper subgroup. For \(C\le Z(E)\) and an embedding \(\varphi\colon C\to Z(H)\) let \(H\circ_CE=(H\times E)/\{(\varphi(z),z^{-1})\colon z\in C\}\). Then \(H'=HZ(E)\) centralises \(E\), \(H\circ_CE=H'\circ E\) is a gluing along all of \(Z(E)\) (with \(\varphi\) the inclusion, so \(s=a^2\in H'\) for \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\)), and \(\gamma_i(H')=\gamma_i(H)\) for \(i\ge2\). For \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\), \(H'\circ E\) can be written as \(H\circ_CE\) with \(C\ne Z(E)\) exactly when \(s\notin\Phi(H')\), which is where the method of part (2) for \(H'\) fails by the remark above. The projection then has to go to \(H\) instead of \(H'\).

Lemma ([Lean]). Let \(K=H\langle r\rangle\) with \(r\) central, \(|K:H|=m\), and \(r^m=\sigma=g^m\) for some \(g\in H\), not necessarily central. Then \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\cap\Delta(K)^n=\Delta(H)^n\) for all \(n\), and \(D_n(K)=D_n(H)\) for \(n\ge2\).

Proof. \(\mathbb{Z}[K]=\bigoplus_{0\le j<m}\mathbb{Z}[H]r^j\); put \(q(\sum_ju_jr^j)=\sum_ju_jg^j\). As \(r^m=g^m\in H\), \(q(ur^j)=ug^j\) for all \(j\in\mathbb{Z}\), so \(q(u\,p(r))=u\,p(g)\) for every Laurent polynomial \(p\). As \(r\) is central, \(\Delta(K)^n\) is spanned by the \(x(r-1)^ir^j\) with \(x\in\Delta(H)^{n-i}\), and \(q(x(r-1)^ir^j)=x(g-1)^ig^j\in\Delta(H)^n\). Hence \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\cap\Delta(K)^n=q(\mathbb{Z}[H]\cap\Delta(K)^n)\subseteq\Delta(H)^n\); the reverse inclusion is clear, and \(D_n(K)\subseteq\gamma_2(K)=\gamma_2(H)\subseteq H\) gives the rest.

For \(m=2\) this is the case \(c=1\) of Proposition 5.8(2). Let \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\), \(C=\langle a^{2^{j+1}}\rangle\) with \(1\le j<k\), and \(\sigma=\varphi(a^{2^{j+1}})\). If \(t\in\gamma_2(H)\) and \(\sigma=g^{2^{j+1}}\) for some \(g\in H\), then \(D_n(H\circ_CE)=D_n(H)\) for \(n\ge2\) [paper]: in the proof of (2) for \(H'\) one has \(H''=H'\langle r\rangle=H\langle r\rangle\) with \(r^{2^{j+1}}=\sigma\) and \(\langle r\rangle\cap H=\langle\sigma\rangle\), so \(|H'':H|=2^{j+1}\), and Lemma 5.9 applies with \(m=2^{j+1}\). For instance, \(H\circ_{\langle t\rangle}M_{16}\) needs \(t=g^4\). The hypothesis \(t\in\gamma_2(H)\) costs nothing for the search: if \(H\circ_CE\) is a candidate, \(t\) is the involution of its cyclic centre, so \(t=n\in\gamma_3(H\circ_CE)=\gamma_3(H)\). [computer] Of the \(386\) candidates of orders \(2^6\)–\(2^9\), \(20\) split as central products (\(5\) of order \(2^8\), \(15\) of order \(2^9\)), with \(212\) factors \(E\) in all. The gluing is proper in \(16\) of these splittings, belonging to \(4\) candidates, always with \(M_{32}\) or \(M_{64}\); Lemma 5.9 covers \(4\) of them. Each of the \(20\) candidates also has a splitting covered by Proposition 5.8, so at these orders a search that skips split candidates does not need proper gluing (code: compute/central, decomp.g; project tracker, D5-29). The other \(12\) splittings would need an analogue of (2) for \(m=4\) (taking \(H\) maximal in \(H'\), i.e. \(j=1\)) with \(g^{-4}\sigma\ne1\); it cannot go through a projection to \(H\) in general, since for \(Q=D_8\circ_{\langle t\rangle}M_{16}\) one has \(\mathbb{Z}[D_8]\cap\Delta(Q)^n\ne\Delta(D_8)^n\) at \(n=4,5\) (index \(4\)), although \(D_n(Q)=D_n(D_8)\) [computer] [open].

\(3\)-torsion. For \(3\)-torsion the computation is no longer needed up to order \(3^7\) (Theorem 5.4(3)); orders \(3^8\) and \(3^9\) and an infinite family are treated in §6. Quotients of the known examples (Rips, \(D_4\ne\gamma_4\) at order \(2^{38}\); Bartholdi–Mikhailov at order \(3^{494}\)) could calibrate how far a counterexample to Question 1.1 must be.

Order \(2^{11}\), all ranks. Proposition. [[computer + paper]; uses [Tah77a, Cor. 19]] \(D_5(Q)=1\) for every \(2\)-group \(Q\) of order \(2^{11}\) and class \(3\). Hence a counterexample to Question 1.1 among finite \(2\)-groups of class \(3\) has order at least \(2^{12}\). Proof. A \(2\)-group of order \(2^{11}\) and class \(3\) with \(D_5\ne1\) is a candidate (above). Ranks \(\ge8\): Proposition 5.7. Ranks \(2\)–\(7\): the searches above find every candidate of these ranks except, at ranks \(5\) and \(6\), those dropped by rule (T), which have \(D_5=1\); all the candidates found have \(D_5=1\). Rank \(1\): cyclic groups are abelian. Orders below \(2^{11}\): Propositions 5.1 and 5.3. See also the remark on the ANUPQ versions above.

Since order \(2^{11}\) is settled, Lemma 5.2 applies to every \(2\)-group \(Q\) of order \(2^{12}\) and class \(3\) with \(D_5(Q)\ne1\) (its quotients by central subgroups of order \(2\) have order \(2^{11}\) and class \(\le3\)). So such a \(Q\) is a candidate, and by Proposition 5.7 it has rank \(d(Q)\le8\) [computer + paper].

Theorem 5.4(3) settles \(3\)-torsion up to order \(3^7\) by metabelianity. Here we go further: we prove \(D_5=\gamma_5\) for all \(3\)-groups of order \(\le 3^9\) (Theorem 6.14) and, on paper, for every finite \(3\)-group \(Q\) with \(Q/\gamma_2(Q)\) of exponent \(3\), of any order (Theorem 6.6). Details, the computations and two independent line-by-line reviews are in the project tracker (D5-26, D5-27); code in compute/magnus. Throughout, the type of a group \(Q\) of class \(c\) is \((a_1,\dots,a_c)\) with \(p^{a_i}=|\gamma_i(Q)/\gamma_{i+1}(Q)|\), and \(L(Q)=\bigoplus_i\gamma_i/\gamma_{i+1}\) is its Lie ring.

text: Lemma. Let \(p\) be odd and \(Q\) a finite \(p\)-group of class \(\le p+1\). Then \(D_{p+2}(Q)\subseteq Q''\cap M_{p+2}(Q)\). In particular, for \(p=3\) and class \(\le4\), \(D_5(Q)\subseteq Q''\cap M_5(Q)\), and \(D_5(Q)\ne1\) needs \(Q''\ne1\), hence \(d(Q)\ge3\).

text: Proof. \(Q/Q''\) is metabelian of class \(\le p+1\), so \(D_{p+2}(Q/Q'')=\gamma_{p+2}(Q/Q'')=1\) by [GT85, Thm. 3.2] (indeed \(D_n(Q/Q'')=\gamma_n(Q/Q'')\) for all \(n\) by [Gup91]), and \(D_{p+2}(Q)\subseteq Q''\) by functoriality. \(D_n\subseteq M_n\) because \(\mathbb{Z}[Q]\to\mathbb F_p[Q]\) maps \(\Delta^n\) into \(\Delta_{\mathbb F_p}^n\). If \(d(Q)\le2\) then \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) is cyclic and \(Q''\subseteq\gamma_5=1\) (see Lemma 6.3).

text: Lemma. [minimal counterexample, \(p=3\)] Let \(Q\) be a \(3\)-group of least order with \(D_5(Q)\ne\gamma_5(Q)\). Then \(Q\) has class \(4\), \(Q''\ne1\) and \(d(Q)\ge3\); \(Z(Q)\) is cyclic and \(D_5(Q)=\Omega_1(Z(Q))=\langle z\rangle\) has order \(3\), with \(z\in Q''\cap M_5(Q)\); the last nontrivial term \(P_c(Q)\) of the lower exponent-\(3\) central series equals \(\langle z\rangle\), so \(Q\) is an immediate descendant of step size \(1\) of \(Q/\langle z\rangle\).

If \(Q\) had class \(\ge5\), then \(Q/\gamma_5(Q)\) would be a smaller counterexample; for class \(\le3\), \(D_5\subseteq D_4=\gamma_4=1\) (Passi: \(D_4=\gamma_4\) without \(2\)-torsion [Pas68]).
